final_answer:
Bottom line: Neither office is favored by the Guidelines themselves. The better strategy is for ONE office to bring a single indictment covering the false claims in both states, rather than two separate prosecutions. Which office that is depends on which district has proper venue over all the counts, which the facts given do not settle. If venue is proper in both, either can do it, and the Guidelines produce the same range.

Reasoning. (1) Guidelines do not differ by district. After Amendment 827 (effective Nov. 1, 2024), 'loss' under USSG 2B1.1(b)(1) is defined in the guideline text as the greater of actual or intended loss. That removes the older Eleventh Circuit (Dupree, en banc, 2023: commentary gets no deference absent genuine ambiguity) versus Fourth Circuit (Boler, 2024: deference to commentary's intended-loss definition) divergence for current-Manual sentencings. Both circuits therefore reach the same 'greater of actual or intended loss' rule, so the circuit of the district gives no reason to choose one office. I did not verify that no residual circuit-specific difference remains for health-care-fraud loss presumptions, so treat that as a caveat. (2) One combined prosecution aggregates the loss. Fraud counts under 2B1.1 are grouped under USSG 3D1.2(d), so the offense level rests on total loss across all counts. Relevant conduct under 1B1.3(a)(2) also reaches acts that are part of the same course of conduct or common scheme or plan, so a court sentencing on one state's counts could consider the other state's conduct too, if it is the same scheme. A single indictment guarantees the combined loss, and the enhancements keyed to it, are in one Guidelines calculation. (3) Separate prosecutions risk wasting the second office's work. If the first-sentenced conduct is relevant conduct to the second case, USSG 5G1.3(b) directs the second court to run its sentence concurrently with the undischarged term and adjust for time served, so the second prosecution adds little. If the conduct is not relevant conduct (two genuinely separate schemes), 5G1.3(d) gives discretion to run consecutively, which could increase total time, but that outcome is discretionary and uncertain, and the defense will argue a single scheme. (4) Statutory cap and stacking. Each 1347 count carries a 10-year maximum (20 if serious bodily injury results). A single indictment with many counts lets 5G1.2(d) stack counts consecutively to reach the total punishment when the Guidelines range exceeds any one count's maximum. This is a further advantage of a single, multi-count indictment. (5) Venue. Under 18 U.S.C. 3237(a), an offense committed in more than one district may be prosecuted in any district where it was begun, continued, or completed. A single district can try both states' claims only if venue is proper for each count there (for example, a common scheme or claims submitted or processed in that district). If the Georgia and South Carolina practices were wholly separate with no connection to the other district, the SC office likely cannot try the Georgia counts and vice versa, and the answer then becomes practical: both districts must prosecute (or one must establish venue), and the Guidelines advantage reduces to sequencing and 5G1.3.

Practical conclusion: Whichever office can lay venue for all counts should indict on everything, charging as many separate executions of the scheme as possible. On facts as given, there is no Guidelines-based reason to prefer SC over GA or the reverse. I could not verify the text of 1B1.3, 5G1.3 or 3237 directly from official sites (access blocked), so those points rest on search-result summaries and should be confirmed against the current Manual and Code.
